displayContract.byline: Assessments made by 5.6 Sol. — Rubric: Slugfester Reassessment Rubric v2.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that the combined explanatory demands presented by contingent existence, apparently objective normativity, and carefully filtered religious experience make a necessary, non-arbitrary transcendent ground a reasonable cumulative inference.

novelty.explanation: This reframes three separate live routes as a modest cumulative inference and repairs their tendency to claim more than each route independently warrants.

premises.text: Contingent reality remains explanatorily incomplete if every member and every derivative structure depends upon conditions that never contain the sufficient basis of actuality within themselves.

novelty.explanation: This replaces an immediate member-to-whole transfer with an explicitly explanatory claim about derivative structures while answering the part-to-whole objection.

premises.text: A terminus of explanation need not be analytically defined into existence; it may instead be inferred posteriorly as nonderivative if dependent reality genuinely requires an ultimate explanatory ground.

novelty.explanation: This preserves experiential inference while avoiding reliance on existence as a predicate or on an a priori ontological definition.

premises.text: Moral criticism presupposes standards that can correct individual feeling and prevailing custom, even though that fact alone does not yet identify those standards with a personal deity.

novelty.explanation: This develops Copleston’s strongest moral point while expressly limiting the conclusion that can be drawn before further theological premises are supplied.

premises.text: Religious experience gains evidential significance only when assessed cumulatively for coherence, independence, lasting transformation, cross-contextual recurrence, and comparative resistance to ordinary psychological explanations.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the original appeal by supplying defeasible discriminatory criteria and by treating transformation as one component rather than verification.

premises.text: If one hypothesis economically explains dependent actuality, objective normative authority, and the best-filtered transcendent experiences together, its cross-domain unification can provide support exceeding any isolated argument.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a cumulative Bayesian-style unification principle that was not expressed as a participant move in the locked transcript inventory.

conclusion.text: Accordingly, a necessary and normatively adequate transcendent ground may be affirmed as the best cumulative explanation if its unified explanatory gain exceeds the strongest naturalistic alternatives, though further argument is required to identify that ground fully with God.

novelty.explanation: The conclusion strengthens all three routes while remaining conditional on comparative success and avoiding an unsupported leap to a fully specified theology.

newArguments.title: Cross-domain explanatory convergence
newArguments.text: The contingency, experiential, and moral routes should be evaluated as partially independent evidence rather than as three demonstrations. A necessary ground addresses why derivative reality exists; a normatively adequate ground addresses why moral criticism can outrun feeling and custom; and a transcendent personal dimension can help explain a carefully filtered class of religious experiences. If one hypothesis predicts these domains with fewer independent assumptions than rival packages, their convergence supplies additional support. This is an abductive comparison, so its force depends on specifying naturalistic competitors and measuring explanatory cost rather than merely repeating that God explains everything.

novelty.explanation: This is a genuinely new cumulative convergence argument, combining independent evidential domains through comparative explanatory economy rather than restating any single transcript inference.

newArguments.title: Normative authority without arbitrary command
newArguments.text: The moral argument can avoid arbitrary divine command by treating goodness as grounded in the stable character of a necessarily good source, while obligations arise from reasons responsive agents have in relation to that good. This account must still compete with secular moral realism, but it explains why obligation can be objective, action-guiding, and resistant to social approval without making goodness whatever a commander happens to decree. The proposal repairs the gap between an objective criterion and God by adding an account of non-arbitrary authority, though it remains a comparative metaphysical hypothesis rather than a direct proof.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the divine-foundation bridge by separating goodness from arbitrary legislation and directly engaging the circularity challenge.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that none of the three domains establishes God because each inference remains underdetermined once modal alternatives, evidential parity, and distinct naturalistic accounts of moral psychology and normativity are separated carefully.

novelty.explanation: This integrates Russell’s objections while repairing the tendency to move from criticism of one inference directly to a comprehensive non-theistic conclusion.

premises.text: Explanations of contingent members do not entail that their totality has a further explanation, and any generalized principle of sufficient reason requires an independent defense rather than intuitive repetition.

novelty.explanation: This develops the totality objection in noncausal terms and directly addresses the broader sufficient-reason formulation identified as the live qualification.

premises.text: Even if dependent reality has an ultimate explanation, additional premises are needed to establish that its terminus is necessary, personal, morally perfect, or appropriately identifiable as God.

novelty.explanation: This introduces an explicit underdetermination ladder between an ultimate explanation and the rich divine conclusion, rather than denying every possible terminus.

premises.text: Private experiences support their interpreted objects only to the extent that publicly assessable features discriminate among incompatible religious, psychological, and cultural explanations.

novelty.explanation: This develops the parity objection into a positive evidential standard instead of treating privacy itself as sufficient grounds for dismissal.

premises.text: Historical variation and social formation can explain why moral attitudes and obligation-feelings differ, but those genealogies must be distinguished from the separate philosophical question of normative validity.

novelty.explanation: This repairs Russell’s conflation of changing belief with truth and of psychological origin with normative authority.

premises.text: Objective moral criticism can be grounded in natural facts about agency, reciprocal justification, suffering, and coherent practical reasons without invoking either raw feeling or divine command.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a substantive secular normative alternative absent from Russell’s brief feeling, custom, and education accounts.

conclusion.text: Therefore, withholding assent to God’s existence is reasonable unless the affirmative case independently defends sufficient reason, supplies discriminatory experiential evidence, and shows that divine grounding explains normative authority better than developed secular alternatives.

novelty.explanation: This converts the skeptical case into a proportionate withholding conclusion tied to explicit unresolved burdens rather than a categorical denial of God.

newArguments.title: The identification gap
newArguments.text: Suppose for argument’s sake that contingent reality has an ultimate nonderivative explanation. That concession does not identify the terminus as conscious, singular, morally perfect, loving, or worthy of worship. Each attribute requires a separate bridge, and some may fit impersonal laws, modal structure, or an unknown metaphysical basis equally well. The affirmative case therefore faces an identification gap after the contingency inference, not merely before it. This argument does not claim that a divine terminus is impossible; it shows that establishing an ultimate ground and establishing God are distinct explanatory achievements whose evidential requirements cannot be merged silently.

novelty.explanation: This new argument isolates the attribute-by-attribute identification problem that remains even after granting an ultimate explanatory terminus.

newArguments.title: Publicly corrigible experience
newArguments.text: Religious experiences may be sincere and personally significant while remaining weak public evidence when their interpretations diverge and lack independent correction procedures. A responsible evidential framework should ask whether predictions, intersubjective checks, or independently confirmed information distinguish transcendent contact from expectation, culture, neurological variation, and memory reconstruction. Transformative benefit can raise practical importance without settling ontology because fictional or mistaken beliefs may also reorganize conduct. This framework improves the skeptical case by specifying what stronger evidence would look like, thereby avoiding the crude inference that an experience is evidentially worthless merely because it is private.

novelty.explanation: This repairs the private-report objection by proposing corrigibility criteria and by allowing limited evidence without granting verification.

newArguments.title: Secular reasons for moral correction
newArguments.text: A naturalistic account need not reduce morality to immediate feeling or inherited taboo. Agents can criticize customs by asking whether principles are coherent, reciprocally justifiable, informed by relevant facts, and responsive to suffering, autonomy, and the conditions of cooperative agency. These standards remain revisable, yet revision does not make them arbitrary any more than revisable scientific methods become mere preference. Such an account answers Copleston’s strongest criticism by explaining how socially formed people can condemn their own society without invoking a transcendent lawgiver. Its remaining burden is to defend why these practical reasons possess authority across divergent agents.

novelty.explanation: This introduces a secular constructivist and reason-based account of objective criticism that goes beyond the participant’s feeling and genealogy arguments.
